flee and abhor, such as all **Salts** <note>original: "Sales"</note>. For we see that if they are thrown into the **Fire** <note>original: "Ignem"</note>, the **Watery Spirit** <term>Spiritus Aqueus</term> <gloss>the vaporous essence of water</gloss> bursts out with a crash before a **Flame** <note>original: "Flamma"</note> is formed. This also occurs gently in leaves that are somewhat resistant, where the watery part bursts out before the oily part catches **Flame**. But this is most clearly seen in **Quicksilver** <term>Argentum vivum</term> <gloss>mercury</gloss>, which is not incorrectly called **Mineral Water** <note>original: "Aqua mineralis"</note>. For this substance, without catching fire, almost equals the powers of **Gunpowder** <term>Pulvis Pyrius</term> <gloss>fiery powder</gloss> through simple eruption and expansion; it is also said that when mixed with gunpowder, it multiplies its powers.

Similarly, let the **Nature under Investigation** <term>Natura Inquisita</term> be the transitory nature of flame and its momentary extinction. For the nature of flame here among us does not seem to be fixed or to endure; instead, it appears to be generated at almost every single moment and immediately extinguished. It is manifest that in flames which continue and last here, that duration does not belong to the same flame as an **Individual** <term>Individuo</term> <gloss>a single, continuous entity</gloss>. Rather, it occurs through a succession of new flames generated one after another; the flame does not remain numerically the same. This is easily perceived from the fact that if the nourishment or **Fuel** <term>fomite</term> <gloss>tinder or kindling</gloss> of the flame is removed, the flame immediately perishes. The **Crossroads** <term>Bivium</term> <note>original: "Bivium"; a logical fork where two paths of explanation diverge.</note> concerning this nature is as follows. This momentary nature occurs either because the **Cause** which first produced it is withdrawing itself, as happens with **Light** <term>Lumen</term>, **Sounds** <term>Sonis</term>, and what they call **Violent Motions** <term>Motibus violentis</term>; or because flame can, by its own nature, remain here among us, but from a con

<summary>Bacon explores the explosive properties of salts and mercury, attributing their power to the expansion of "watery spirits" rather than combustion. He also characterizes flame as a continuous succession of new events rather than a single lasting body, comparing its persistence to light and sound.</summary>
